hook.prompt: What exactly was the “puzzle” of the 1965 election?
options: The polls showed the SPD ahead, but the CDU/CSU won the election.
Voting intentions hardly moved for months; meanwhile the expectation of “who will win?” drifted in one direction, and in the end the votes drifted that way too.
Most voters did not answer the poll, so the result could not be predicted in advance.
Both parties got almost exactly 50 percent.
hook.explain: The puzzle was not a “polling error” but a split between two measures: voting intention was steady, expectation of the winner was moving. That is why the first option looks tempting but is wrong: the polls showed a neck-and-neck race in voting intention, not the SPD ahead. And the result (47.6 percent against 39.3) was not a “fifty-fifty” one either.

context-ideas.prompt: Your friend says: “public opinion is the shared reason that comes out of a calm debate among smart citizens.” How would Noelle-Neumann respond to this view?
options: She would agree entirely; public opinion is the product of rational debate.
She would see public opinion above all as a means of social control that binds the individual to the community, and she would reject this view.
She would say there is no such thing as public opinion.
She would treat public opinion merely as a numerical total measured in polls.
context-ideas.explain: Noelle-Neumann’s Mainz inaugural lecture defines public opinion precisely as social control. Measuring with poll numbers is her tool, but her definition of public opinion is not a numerical total; so the last option looks tempting but is wrong. The first option is the view she opposed.

noelle-neumann-life.prompt: According to this card, how did Noelle-Neumann’s running a polling institute while also working at a university help her theory?
options: She took the theory from the university and applied it at Allensbach; field data did not become part of the theory.
Field survey data (Allensbach) and theoretical questions (the university) came together in one person; the theory fed on both sources.
The theory was written entirely in Missouri, in the United States, and brought to Germany later.
The theory was published in her name by a student of Lazarsfeld.
noelle-neumann-life.explain: The card says that staying at the head of Allensbach fed the theory from both the field and the university. What she met in Missouri was Gallup polls and the pressure to conform; the theory itself grew out of election observations in Germany in the 1960s and 1970s. Lazarsfeld was only her scientific model.

timeline.prompt: Put the events in the right order (oldest to newest).
items: The German election in which expectations shifted while voting intention stayed steady (1965)
The spiral of silence article in the Journal of Communication (1974)
The English edition The Spiral of Silence (1984)
timeline.explain: First the observation (1965), then the first publications (1974), then the German book (1980) and its English edition (1984). The most common mistake is to take the English edition for the “first book” and swap 1980 and 1984.

claim.prompt: According to the theory, what actually drives the spiral?
options: A view really being in the majority.
People perceiving that a view is in the majority or on the rise.
The government banning a view.
The number of people defending a view increasing.
claim.explain: The theory foregrounds the perceived distribution: in 1965 too, expectations shifted while the parties’ real strength had not changed. The real majority (first option) is a tempting answer, but the theory’s interesting claim is precisely that the real and the perceived distribution can come apart. A ban is a legal, not a social, pressure.

myth-silence.prompt: According to the theory, a person who thinks their opinion is in the minority will necessarily change their mind as well as staying silent in public.
myth-silence.explain: False. The theory predicts public behaviour, that is, silence; the opinion may well stay the same inside, and the theory does not rule this out. When this distinction is lost, the ‘spiral’ gets mixed up with ‘persuasion’.

concept-isolation.prompt: Which description of “public opinion” is closest to Noelle-Neumann’s definition?
options: The opinion that gets the most votes in an election.
The conclusion reached by rational debate among experts.
The opinions a person can express openly on contested issues without being excluded.
The opinion that newspapers put in their headlines.
concept-isolation.explain: The definition links what can be said openly with not being excluded. An election result and expert debate are other conceptions of public opinion (the second, in particular, is the ‘rational debate’ view Noelle-Neumann opposed). Headlines are the media’s business; in the theory the media influence the climate, but that is not the definition of public opinion.

concept-climate.prompt: What does the question “Whatever your own opinion, what do you think most people think about this issue?” measure?
options: The person’s own attitude.
The climate of opinion the person perceives (the present state).
The person’s willingness to speak out.
How long the person spends using media.
concept-climate.explain: The question deliberately asks not for the person’s own opinion but for their perception of their surroundings. Willingness to speak out is a separate measurement (the train test); attitude is measured by a separate question. The theory says these three measures are distinct from one another, and that the spiral comes out of precisely this distinction.

options: Those who defend the majority’s opinion most loudly.
Those who hide their opinion and conform to the majority.
The minority who go on defending their opinion, accepting exclusion (or because they are already excluded).
Experts who appear in the media.
concept-speak-hardcore.explain: The hard core is the exception to the spiral: the minority that does not fall silent. Those who loudly defend the majority make up the visible side that is the result of the spiral; those who hide their opinion are the ones caught in the spiral. There is no link between being an expert and being the hard core.

five-assumptions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the theory’s basic assumptions?
options: Society threatens the deviant individual with exclusion.
Individuals constantly feel fear of isolation.
The media always reflect the majority’s opinion accurately.
The individual tries to assess the climate of opinion.
five-assumptions.explain: The third option is not among the five; it is also against the spirit of the theory, because the theory assumes that the media can distort the climate of opinion and so make a minority look like a majority. The other three are, respectively, assumptions 1, 2 and 3 of the five.

asch-thread.prompt: What did Noelle-Neumann mainly use Asch’s line experiments for in her theory?
options: To prove that the media directly influence the audience.
To support the idea that people are uncomfortable standing alone against a group, that is, the reality of fear of isolation.
To develop the train test that measures willingness to speak out.
To show how large the hard core group is.
asch-thread.explain: As Griffin reports, Asch is used as one of the psychological supports for fear of isolation. The experiment has nothing directly to do with media influence or the train test; and since in Asch too most answers remained independent, it is not a tool for measuring the size of the hard core either.

conditions.prompt: Where a society fully agrees on an issue, the spiral of silence is expected to work strongly.
conditions.explain: False. The spiral starts on contested issues, when opposing views exist; with full consensus there is no minority opinion to silence. The right answer follows from the principle that the theory is not considered valid on every issue.

spiral-steps.prompt: For the spiral to advance, the actual number of supporters of the silent side must also have fallen.
spiral-steps.explain: False. What turns the spiral is the visibility gap: even if the silent side stays the same in number, it looks small in the public sphere and this appearance produces new silences. A fall in numbers can be a result of the spiral, not a precondition.

media.prompt: A news channel has for years emphasised the same opinion in a debate. According to the theory, what does this change most?
options: It forcibly changes viewers’ personal attitudes one by one.
Which opinion is perceived as widespread and established, that is, the climate of opinion, and so willingness to speak out openly.
It only determines which issue is seen as important.
It changes nothing, because everyone is selective.
media.explain: The theory’s media claim concerns the perception of the climate. The “only the order of importance” answer describes agenda-setting, but the spiral goes a step further and claims which opinion seems speakable. The last option is exactly the ‘selective perception neutralises everything’ view that Noelle-Neumann objected to.

lab-group-chat.prompt: In this thought experiment, which of the following has NOT happened?
options: Side A becoming more visible in the public sphere.
Most of side B falling silent.
Side B really changing their minds.
The group misperceiving B’s real size.
lab-group-chat.explain: That is exactly the trick of the experiment: visibility and perception changed, opinions did not. The other three are the workings of the spiral itself. This is why the theory’s distinction between ‘staying silent’ and ‘changing your mind’ matters.

evidence-1972.prompt: According to Petersen’s account, how was the “visibility gap” the theory predicts observed in 1972?
options: CDU/CSU supporters wore more badges and stuck more stickers.
SPD supporters were visible in badges, stickers and arguments; CDU/CSU supporters, equal in number, were almost invisible in public.
Both sides were equally visible.
SPD supporters were silent, CDU/CSU supporters were loud.
evidence-1972.explain: In 1972 the expectation favoured the SPD, and visibility favoured the SPD too. The first option is closer to the mood of 1965 (the expectation that the CDU/CSU would win); 1972 is its ‘reverse’. The theory’s strength is that the same mechanism can work in opposite directions in two elections.

evidence-train.prompt: What exactly does the train test measure?
options: What a person actually does on a real train journey.
A person’s declaring how willing they are to state their opinion in an imaginary situation.
The intensity of a person’s fear of isolation, directly.
How much a person is exposed to the media.
evidence-train.explain: The train test measures a declaration in response to an imaginary scenario: not real behaviour, but willingness to speak. Fear of isolation is not measured directly by this test; it is inferred from the theory, and this is exactly one of the points of criticism of the theory.

critique-measurement.prompt: What is the most fundamental criticism of the train test?
options: That it is too expensive.
That it measures declared willingness in an imaginary situation, not real behaviour.
That it can only be applied to young people.
That it does not take media influence into account at all.
critique-measurement.explain: The criticism concerns the gap between declaration and behaviour; this is why Glynn and colleagues recommend observing real willingness to speak in future. Options such as cost and age limits do not appear as criticisms in either Griffin or Scheufele–Moy.

critique-verdict.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall picture from the meta-analyses?
options: The theory has been definitively refuted; there is no relationship between perceived support and willingness to speak.
The theory has been fully proven; the relationship is very strong.
The relationship is small but not zero and consistent across many studies; the mechanism (especially fear and the cycle over time) is still not sufficiently tested.
The meta-analyses found a relationship only online.
critique-verdict.explain: In both the 1997 and the 2018 meta-analyses the relationship comes out small but significant; online it is no weaker either. The ‘refuted’ and ‘proven’ answers miss this middle ground. The last option contradicts the finding of Matthes and colleagues.

critique-person.prompt: Which is correct about the relationship between evaluating the theory and the debate over Noelle-Neumann’s Nazi-era past?
options: The biographical debate automatically refutes the theory.
Whether the theory holds up against data is a separate question from the biographical debate; the two should be assessed separately.
The biographical debate is completely irrelevant and should never be mentioned.
The theory can only be evaluated once the biographical debate is settled.
critique-person.explain: The two questions are answered with different methods: empirical tests and historical research. One does not automatically refute the other; so the first and fourth options are wrong. But the biography is not entirely irrelevant either: Wendelin uses these elements in placing the theory in terms of sociology of knowledge.

today-pew.prompt: How can the Pew finding be related to the spiral of silence theory?
options: It proves the theory conclusively, because Facebook users spoke less.
It refutes the theory, because 86 percent were willing to speak.
It is a clue supporting the link between perceived climate (does my circle agree?) and willingness to speak in an online context; but it is limited to a single issue and declared willingness.
It has nothing to do with the theory; the Snowden surveillance issue is outside the spiral’s scope.
today-pew.explain: Pew found a link between perceived agreement and willingness to speak, and saw an online/offline difference. But since it is one issue, one moment and declared willingness, it neither ‘proves’ nor ‘refutes’. According to the theory, contested and emotionally charged issues are within scope; the surveillance debate is such an issue.

today-online.prompt: According to this card, everyone being able to speak in online environments has abolished the spiral of silence.
today-online.explain: False. The studies in the card show that the relationship persists online (Matthes and colleagues), that the perception of surveillance can lower willingness to speak (Stoycheff), and that some users can both hold back and feel freer online (Kutlu). The stage changed; the mechanism did not disappear.

turkey-studies.prompt: Which is correct about Kutlu’s (2019) Facebook study?
options: It was done with a random sample representing all Facebook users in Turkey.
It was done with 404 users in İstanbul using snowball sampling; so the results cannot be generalised to Turkey as a whole.
It was done only with the experimental (laboratory) method.
It re-analysed Noelle-Neumann’s 1965 data.
turkey-studies.explain: Snowball sampling finds participants through one another’s acquaintances; it is not representative. So the findings (positive relationships) are a clue, not a generalisation to Turkey as a whole. The study is a survey; it is neither an experiment nor a re-analysis of the 1965 data.

turkey-karaca.prompt: Why might a newspaper’s reports being in line with the dominant view not, by itself, count as proof of the spiral of silence?
options: Because newspapers have no interest in the theory.
Because the same agreement can also arise from other mechanisms, such as legal bans and censorship, rather than from social fear of isolation.
Because the theory holds only on social media.
Because Cumhuriyet was not published in the 1980s.
turkey-karaca.explain: The theory’s mechanism is social fear of isolation; legal pressure in the coup period can also produce a similar silence. So saying ‘similar outcome = same mechanism’ is a wrong inference. The option saying the theory is limited to social media is wrong: the theory was developed in the 1960s in the context of mass media.

exam-patterns.prompt: In the Turkish course text, which event does the “case example” section of the spiral of silence theory describe?
options: The 1965 German elections
The 1980 US presidential election (Carter–Reagan)
The 1940 Erie County voter study
The 1968 Chapel Hill agenda-setting study
exam-patterns.explain: In Polat’s text, 10.2.1 is “Örnek Olay: Almanya’da 1965 Meclis Seçimleri” (“Case Example: The 1965 Parliamentary Elections in Germany”). The 1980 US election is the opening example of some English textbooks (a trap); the Erie County voter study is a classic of the limited-effects and selective-exposure debate, and Chapel Hill is the classic of agenda-setting.

exam-pairs.prompt: Match the name or institution on the left with the correct description.
pairs: Noelle-Neumann
Author of the spiral of silence article published in the Journal of Communication in 1974
Asch
Conductor of the line-length conformity experiments (1950s)
Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan
The 1997 meta-analysis pooling studies on the relationship between perceived support and willingness to speak
Scheufele and Moy
The 2000 conceptual review of the theory’s first quarter-century
Allensbach
The polling institute Noelle-Neumann founded in 1947
exam-pairs.explain: The confusion is usually between Asch and Noelle-Neumann: Asch ran the experiment; Noelle-Neumann developed the theory and used Asch as background. The meta-analysis (Glynn and colleagues) and the conceptual review (Scheufele and Moy) are also different types: one is a numerical pooling, the other a review of concepts and measurement.

summary.text: In the spiral of silence theory the engine is fear of {{1}}. What drives the spiral is not the real distribution of opinions but the {{2}} distribution. The German book came out in {{3}}, the English edition in {{4}}.

options: loneliness
isolation
punishment
shame
perceived
actual
legal
measured

summary.explain: The theory’s engine is fear of isolation; the spiral works through the perceived distribution. The German book came out in 1980, the English edition in 1984 (1974 is the article, and 1993 is the date of the second English edition).

quiz.prompt: Which is the spiral of silence theory’s first scholarly article in English?
options: Noelle-Neumann, “The spiral of silence: A theory of public opinion”, Journal of Communication, 1974
Noelle-Neumann, “The Spiral of Silence: Public Opinion – Our Social Skin”, 1984
Asch, “Studies of independence and conformity”, 1956
Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan, “Perceived support for one’s opinions and willingness to speak out”, 1997
quiz.explain: The theory was first published in English in the 1974 Journal of Communication article. The 1984 work is not an article but the English edition of the German book; Asch’s monograph is a conformity study in the theory’s background; and Glynn and colleagues is a meta-analysis testing the theory.

quiz.prompt: A student does not state their opinion openly in an emotionally charged debate because they think most of the class is against them. What mainly explains this behaviour in the theory?
options: Fear of isolation
Cognitive dissonance
The student having really changed their mind
Censorship applied by the state
quiz.explain: The theory’s engine is the fear of isolation of a person who thinks they are in the minority. Having changed their mind (third option) looks tempting, but the theory predicts silence, not a change of mind. Censorship is a legal, not a social, pressure.

quiz.prompt: Noelle-Neumann’s German book Die Schweigespirale was published in 1984 and its English edition in 1980.
quiz.explain: The reverse is true: the German book came out in 1980 (Piper), the English edition in 1984 (University of Chicago Press). Because the English edition is a translation of the German one, it comes later.

quiz.prompt: According to the theory, an opinion can look strong or weak in the public sphere even if the real number of its supporters does not change at all.
quiz.explain: True. What drives the spiral is not the real but the perceived distribution of opinions: an opinion defended loudly looks stronger than it is, the silent side looks weaker than it is. The 1965 and 1972 observations are the starting point of this claim.

quiz.prompt: Match the terms with the correct descriptions.
pairs: Climate of opinion
The perception of which opinion is widespread or rising in one’s surroundings
Quasi-statistical sense
The ability to sense the distribution and trend of opinion around one without running a poll
Hard core
The minority that keeps voicing its opinion, accepting exclusion
Train test
A method for measuring willingness to speak using an imaginary journey scenario
Fear of isolation
The worry of falling out of one’s surroundings’ favour, which sets the spiral in motion
quiz.explain: The climate of opinion is the perceived distribution, and the quasi-statistical sense is the sense that detects this distribution; confusing the two is a common mistake. The train test measures the spiral’s outcome (willingness to speak), not the fear. The hard core is the exception to the spiral.

quiz.prompt: Put the spiral’s workings in the right order.
items: An issue becomes contested and people probe the climate of opinion
Those who think their opinion is gaining ground speak; those who think they are in the minority fall silent
The speaking side looks bigger than its real strength, the silent side looks smaller
This appearance becomes a new climate signal and the process accelerates for another round
quiz.explain: First the climate is probed, then comes the decision to speak or stay silent, then the visibility gap appears and this gap becomes the input of the next round. That is the spiral: the output returns as input.

quiz.text: In the 1965 German election, {{1}} stayed steady for months, but the expectation {{2}} shifted toward the CDU/CSU. Noelle-Neumann explained this with a theory based on fear of {{3}}.

options: voting intention
turnout
the number of polls
media budgets
about who would win
about when the election would be held
about turnout
about media budgets
isolation
punishment
poverty
censorship

quiz.explain: The puzzle was the split between voting intention and the winner expectation; Noelle-Neumann’s answer was fear of isolation. Punishment and censorship are legal mechanisms, whereas the theory describes social pressure.

quiz.scenario: (Hypothetical example.) On a university campus, on an emotionally charged and contested issue, one opinion is defended constantly and loudly on social media. Many students disagree with this opinion, but most do not write comments. One student, thinking “Everyone thinks like this”, gives up sharing their own different opinion.

parts.prompt: Which concept of the theory does the student’s belief that “everyone thinks like this” correspond to?
options: The perceived climate of opinion
Hard core
Meta-analysis
Cultivation
parts.explain: The student’s perception of the distribution of opinion around them, that is, the perception of the climate of opinion, is at work here. The hard core is the minority that does not fall silent; this student is going silent. A meta-analysis is a method, and cultivation is another theory.

parts.prompt: Even though the number of students who disagree with the opinion is really large, why does the opinion look widespread?
options: The visibility gap: the speaking side looks bigger than its real strength, the silent side looks small.
The majority is forcibly silencing the others.
The students really changed their minds.
There is a legal ban.
parts.explain: The theory ties silence to a social visibility gap: silence changes not the number but the appearance. Forced silencing and bans are different mechanisms; and a change of mind is not what the theory predicts.

parts.prompt: In evaluating this scenario, which objection of the critics is particularly important?
options: The climate of the immediate circle (friends, family, class) may determine willingness to speak more than the general social media climate.
The theory holds only for television.
The Asch experiment was never conducted.
Willingness to speak cannot be measured on social media.
parts.explain: According to the critics, rather than the country’s or the platform’s climate, the climate of the immediate circle may be decisive. The claim that the theory is specific to television is not true; Asch’s experiment was conducted; willingness to speak has also been measured on social media, though the distinction between declaration and behaviour still matters.

quiz.takeaway: The perception of the climate, the visibility gap and the reference group should be thought about together: what drives the spiral is appearance more than numbers, and which climate a person takes into account can vary from person to person.

quiz.prompt: A researcher measures willingness to speak with the train test and says “the role of fear of isolation in the theory has been proven”. Which criticism is most directly aimed at this inference?
options: Fear of isolation was not measured in this test but assumed; also the test measures an imaginary situation.
The test is too expensive.
The theory can never be tested outside Germany.
Asch’s experiment is wrong.
quiz.explain: Fear being assumed rather than measured, and the test being imaginary, are the theory’s two basic measurement criticisms. Cost or geographic-limit criticisms do not appear in the literature; and Asch’s experiment is the theory’s background and is not discussed here.

quiz.prompt: Which Turkish-language name or names do the Turkish course books use for the spiral of silence? (Polat’s unit title says “Sessizlik Sarmalı”, his section title says “Suskunluk Sarmalı Kuramı”, and Yaylagül writes “Suskunluk Sarmalı”; “sessizlik” and “suskunluk” are both Turkish words for “silence”.)
options: Both “Suskunluk Sarmalı” and “Sessizlik Sarmalı” occur, depending on the book; they all name the same theory of Noelle-Neumann’s.
“Sessizlik Sarmalı” and “Suskunluk Sarmalı” are two different theories.
“Sessizlik Sarmalı” is Asch’s theory and “Suskunluk Sarmalı” is Noelle-Neumann’s.
Only the theory Yaylagül describes, “Suskunluk Sarmalı”, is Noelle-Neumann’s.
quiz.explain: The names vary from book to book, but the theory is the same. This lesson uses “spiral of silence” throughout for consistency. The other options are traps: a differently written name does not mean a different theory.

quiz.scenario: A researcher is examining a newspaper’s reports in a post-coup period. Although the newspaper describes itself as oppositional, it has written reports in line with the official discourse. The researcher presents this as “the existence of a spiral of silence”.

parts.prompt: What is the weakest point of this inference?
options: It has not been distinguished whether the cause of the agreement is social fear of isolation or legal pressure and censorship.
The newspaper being oppositional is irrelevant to the theory.
News analysis is never scientific.
There cannot be a spiral of silence in coup periods.
parts.explain: The theory’s mechanism is social fear of isolation; legal pressure can produce a similar silence. So saying ‘similar outcome = same mechanism’ weakens the inference. The other options are either contrary to fact or overgeneralisations.

parts.prompt: What could be done to strengthen the inference?
options: Trying to separate out the effect of legal restrictions and directly measuring journalists’ or readers’ fear of isolation and willingness to speak.
Counting a few more reports with the same method.
Focusing on a single report only.
Interpreting the results so as to make them consistent with the theory.
parts.explain: The way to separate the two explanations is to control for the effect of legal pressure and to measure fear directly. Counting more reports enlarges the same uncertainty; focusing on a single report and making the result fit the theory are biased routes of inference.

quiz.takeaway: A similar outcome does not mean the same mechanism: when applying the theory to real events, alternative explanations must be separated out.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct about Matthes and colleagues’ 2018 meta-analysis (66 studies, over 27,000 participants)?
options: The relationship is small (about r = .10) but different from zero; it is no weaker online than offline.
The relationship is very strong (r about .80).
It covers only offline studies.
It definitively refutes the theory.
quiz.explain: The meta-analysis finds a small but consistent relationship and sees no weakening online. Extreme readings such as r = .80 or ‘definitive refutation’ do not match the finding; and the studies include both online and offline settings.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct about Asch’s 1956 monograph?
options: It was done with 123 subjects; about a third of the estimates in the critical trials moved to the majority’s wrong answer, but most estimates remained independent and some subjects never conformed.
Most subjects conformed to the majority in every trial.
In the control group too about a third of the estimates were wrong.
The experiment was done with only a single confederate.
quiz.explain: Asch’s data show both conformity and independence: of 123 subjects, 94 conformed at least once and 29 never did. In the control group errors were under 1 percent, and in the main experiment the majority was 7–9 people.
